stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In trials at forty accounting and software firms, employees moved to a four-day week with no cut in pay. Managers reported that output held steady while sick days and reported burnout fell. Advocates concluded that a shorter week benefits workers and employers alike.

Text 2
The office trials are encouraging, but they may not describe every workplace. When a regional hospital laundry tried the same schedule, its machines still needed staff every day, so the remaining shifts grew longer and output fell by nearly a tenth.
choices: It identifies a workplace where the result reported in Text 1 did not hold.
It offers further evidence that output held steady under a shorter week.
It argues that a four-day week reduces output in nearly every kind of job.
It describes the office trials that the advocates in Text 1 had criticized.
explanation: Text 1 reports a general result: at office firms, output held steady under a four-day week, and advocates say everyone benefits. Text 2 starts by crediting those trials ("encouraging"), then turns to one workplace, a hospital laundry, where output fell. So Text 2 limits the scope of Text 1's claim without rejecting it.

B.why: You picked up the shared topic but missed the turn at "but." At the laundry output fell, so Text 2 does not support the steady-output finding.

C.why: You turned one counterexample into a sweeping rule. Text 2 describes one laundry and calls the office results encouraging, so it never says nearly every job loses output.

D.why: You assigned the wrong role to Text 1. The advocates praised the office trials and did not criticize them. This choice gets Text 2's subject right and Text 1's position wrong.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Between 2015 and 2020, twelve towns installed chilled water fountains in their public parks. Over the same period, surveys showed that children in those towns drank about a third less soda. The researchers therefore concluded that easy access to free water led children to choose it over sugary drinks.

Text 2
No one doubts that soda drinking fell in these towns. Yet most of them also banned soda sales in their schools during those years, and that policy could simply have produced the drop on its own.
choices: It questions whether soda drinking among the children actually declined.
It proposes a different possible cause for the decline described in Text 1.
It presents survey results showing that the fountains raised soda drinking.
It explains the method the researchers in Text 1 used to survey children.
explanation: Text 1 ends with its conclusion ("therefore"): the fountains caused the decline. Text 2 accepts that the decline happened ("No one doubts..."). It then names another explanation, the school soda bans, that "could simply" account for the same result. Text 2 agrees on the observation and offers a different cause.

A.why: You read Text 2 as disagreeing about everything. Its first sentence grants that soda drinking fell. It disputes only the cause.

C.why: You invented a finding that reverses both texts. Neither text reports that soda drinking rose, and Text 2 presents no new survey.

D.why: You fixed on the word "surveys" in Text 1. Text 2 never discusses how the data were gathered. It is about what caused the drop.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Many astronomers think that "hot Jupiters," giant planets that orbit extremely close to their stars, could not have formed there, since too little gas exists so near a star. Instead, these planets are thought to have formed far out and then migrated inward over millions of years.

Text 2
The planet WR-208b offers a telling case. Its orbit is sharply tilted relative to its star's equator, a pattern that a planet forming close in would be unlikely to show but that a long inward journey would readily produce.
choices: It presents a general theory that the planet discussed in Text 1 illustrates.
It describes a planet that appears to have formed close to its own star.
It gives a specific example that is consistent with the view in Text 1.
It explains why astronomers first began searching for giant planets.
explanation: Text 1 states a general view: hot Jupiters formed far out and migrated inward. Text 2 describes one planet, WR-208b ("a telling case"), whose tilted orbit is what a long inward journey would produce. Text 2 is a specific example that supports Text 1's general claim.

A.why: You reversed the roles. Text 1 holds the general theory and Text 2 holds the single planet. Text 1 discusses no specific planet.

B.why: You took the opposite of Text 2's point. Text 2 says a planet forming close in would be unlikely to have this orbit, so WR-208b points toward migration.

D.why: You answered a question neither text raises. The history of planet searches does not appear in Text 2. It is about one planet's orbit.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologists have long cautioned that earthquakes cannot be predicted with any useful precision. Small tremors occur constantly, and only rarely does one turn out to be a foreshock to a major quake, so no one can say in advance when a large rupture will strike.

Text 2
Although the exact timing of large quakes remains beyond reach, warning is still possible. Sensors can detect the fast, weak first waves of a quake that has already begun and send alerts seconds before the slower, damaging waves arrive, time enough to halt trains.
choices: It accepts Text 1's point about prediction but describes another kind of warning.
It claims that new sensors can now predict when large quakes will occur.
It gives an example of a small tremor that turned out to be a foreshock.
It rejects the alert sensors that the seismologists in Text 1 had recommended.
explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession ("Although the exact timing... remains beyond reach"), which agrees with Text 1 that quakes cannot be predicted. It then turns to a different kind of warning: detecting a quake that has already started and alerting people seconds before the damaging waves arrive.

B.why: You missed the concession. Text 2 says timing remains beyond reach. The sensors detect a quake that has already begun and do not predict one.

C.why: You fixed on a detail from Text 1. Foreshocks appear only in Text 1, and Text 2 gives no example of one.

D.why: You attributed something to Text 1 that it does not say. Text 1 never mentions or recommends alert sensors, and Text 2 supports them.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Folklorists studying modern urban legends have argued that such stories spread because they give voice to shared anxieties. Tales of contaminated fast food, for instance, circulated most widely as families began relying on meals prepared by unseen strangers.

Text 2
Nineteenth-century sailors' accounts of sea serpents fit a similar pattern. Reports of the creatures multiplied in decades when shipwrecks were frequent and crossings felt especially perilous, suggesting that the tales expressed fears crews could not otherwise name.
choices: It disputes Text 1's claim that legends express widely shared anxieties.
It extends the explanation in Text 1 to stories from an earlier period.
It offers the general theory that the examples in Text 1 then illustrate.
It argues that sailors' reports of sea serpents were largely accurate.
explanation: Text 1 explains that legends spread because they express shared anxieties, and it gives a modern example. Text 2 says sailors' tales "fit a similar pattern" and applies the same explanation to stories from the 1800s. Text 2 extends Text 1's idea to an earlier era.

A.why: You missed the agreement signal. "Fit a similar pattern" tells you Text 2 accepts Text 1's explanation and uses it.

C.why: You reversed which text does what. Text 1 states the general theory, and Text 2 supplies another case of it.

D.why: You read in a claim Text 2 never makes. It treats the sightings as expressions of fear and never says the serpents were real.
